Jetboils are fine if you're wanting to boil water, fast, and don't mind the weight, and are willing to lose the speed and the efficiency if you're going to camp anywhere with anything more than a breeze. For roughly the same price I can get an MSR micro rocket or gigapeak and something like an evernew Ti pot and save half a pound or more on my cook kit.

The Jetboil is pretty much only usable by jetboil systems. You're locked in.

Well first note that it is designed to use trekking poles. I can't remember if the site has stand alone poles, but those will obviously add to the weight.

Setup- Stake the 4 corners out. The tent has a bathtub with carbon fiber stays in it which are awesome for keeping the bathtub floor a bathtub floor. The top corners loop over your stakes (this is a little trickier if you can't stake things down. You're going to need rocks or extra line or some creativity to do it. I talked to a woman who pitched the solong on AT camping platforms using cordage and rocks). Then you unzip the tent, and there's a little plastic/carbon fiber stay in there that's bent (I think it's rigid plastic) at just the right angle that velcros in. Take your hiking pole, stick the tip in the  plastic tube, and shove the round handle down into the middle of the tent. Repeat on other side. I usually crawl in, hold it up, and pitch that way. Adjust height for tauntness.

You're basically done at that point. The awning rolls up or pulls down and can be propped open with a stick. Dropping it into storm mode is basically as easy as Pulling the stick out and maybe having a stake or a rock or branch or something to tie down on. Pretty easy. 

It takes a little getting used to and you absolutely want to pitch it a few times in your back yard before getting out on the trail. Make sure you use a tyvek groundsheet (you can order one from the website if you don't want to dick with it) because the ground bathtub is silnylon and pretty thin. It's just safer to pitch on top of a groundsheet. 

In better weather you can roll back the awnings and get some real airflow through the tent, which is another reason I like it. 

I'm really happy with the tent. I haven't met anyone who didn't like the design.

Edit: Okay so here's the epidemic rules:  
1. Increase the infection draw rate token one space

2. Infect: Draw a city from the bottom of the deck and put 3 cubes on it. Discard this city into the discard pile

3. Intensify: shuffle the infection discard pile and place it on the top of the infection deck.

Proceed with turn as normal (usually either drawing one more card or proceeding to the infect stage). 

 

Basically, after the first epidemic, the game is going to concern itself with mostly the cities that you've already seen develop diseases, with the occasional epidemic throwing a new city into the mix for giggles. Depending on how the epidemics were loaded into the deck at the beginning of the game, you may see more cities as you get higher infection rates and have more than your average turns between epidemics. But the cities that you pull at the start of the game until your first epidemic are always going to be your worst "problem" cities. They'll always keep showing up.
To be specific, don't shuffle the discard directly into the infection deck, shuffle the discards and then place on *top* of the infection deck.

The next time you go through an infection phase, [Location] is now on top of the deck and may get a cube added to it. Then it gets discarded and stays out of play until the next epidemic. Then it goes back into play and is at risk again.

Ayup. At a certain point you care based on traffic shaping, firewalls, ACLs, etc... But at a rudimentary level, you really don't care what kind of data is being sent.

As for why B accepts data from A, at a networking level the frames  and packets are announcing that they are destined for computer B. The NIC verifies that the frames are indeed for it, the OS verifies that the IP is indeed it's own. Depending on if the traffic is TCP or UDP there may be some bi-directional communication between the computers to facilitate data transfer but again, that's higher level than probably you're dealing with at this point.

The OSI model breaks down how data is sent from Computer A to Computer B. You need to learn it and understand it. I've been doing this for 20 years now almost and I still go back to the OSI model to conceptualize WTF is going on when troubleshooting.

&#x200B;

> I never really get what people mean by saying they want to send data to another network. 

Data means all the parts of a frame or packet that aren't used for navigation. So for a frame, anything that is not the destination MAC, source MAC, ethernet type, or checksum is the data. At the switch level, it never looks at the "data" payload.  For a packet it's similar, but the construction of a packet has different fields. But again, for the level that you're at, we don't even look at the data payload. Something further up the OSI model will look at that. 

Understanding encapsulation and decapsulation is important.

Layer 6 & 7 are the Operating System infrastructure and applications. Let's say you're playing a game with a game server. You need to send information to the server on what you're doing. So the game client & OS are essentially layers 6 & 7 and kind of beyond our scope. The application creates a protocol data unit of "game instructions" and hands that off to the networking protocol stack in the OS. The OS then whacks those up into UDP datagrams (TCP has bi-directional communication and we aren't going there yet, UDP is just best effort but generally faster. Layers 6 & 7 have to detect data loss and re-request data, where as TCP can detect lost data and request a retransmission). It then hands off the datagrams, which include a destination, to the IP stack, who encapsulates the UDP datagram into an IP packet. This packet has source and destination network info, and uses the logical IP addresses. It will chunk up the UDP datagram into multiple packets because the TCP packets are smaller than the UDP datagrams. It will then pass the packets on to the layer 2 NIC processor, who will whack up the packets into smaller frames and encapsulate them with destination and source addresses and a checksum. These addresses are MAC addresses- hardware addresses on the NIC. The NIC then takes these frames and passes them off to the Layer 1 portion of the NIC, which generates electrical impulses across the wire.

Let's say you're plugged into the router directly. The router picks up the electrical signals and it's ethernet port and reassembles them into frames. It then looks at the frame destination and says "Yup! that's for me!" otherwise it drops the packet and ignores it. But this is a good packet, so it strips off the frame header and tail and decapsulates it, leaving just the data. It then passes that up to the TCP level of the router, who assembles the data frame payloads into a packet. It then looks at the packet's destination address and determines what port to send the packet out. It routes the packet out to that port, whacks it back into frames to hop to the next router's interface/MAC (assuming we're using ethernet all the way), and then the port breaks down the data into electrical impulses and sends the data as bits and bytes. The next router does the same thing, reassembling the frame, then making sure it should be the right destination before stripping the frame delivery information and passing the data back up to the router to assemble into layer 3 packets. The router says "Hey! This packet is on my network!" and routs it out the local network interface, following the same process. It then re-encapsulates everything down to frames and then forwards the bits and bytes out.

Computer B gets these bits, and then reassembles them. It looks at the frame and says "Yup that's me!" and strips the frame information off and passes the data up to layer 3. IP layer 3 reassembles the packets and looks at the destination IP and says "yup! That's me!" and pulls off all the IP transit information and hands it up to layer 4/5 UDP, who takes the packets and assembles them into UDP datagrams and says "Cool story bro, this looks like a good datagram for a port that I have open" and strips the UDP information off and then hands it off to the OS, who says "Oh this is meant for the game! Here you go game client" who finally analyzes that you've  clicked your mouse button to swing your axe. Now the game client needs to tell Computer A "message received" or "send that again please" and the whole process repeats in reverse and so on ad nauseum.

&#x200B;

Congrats. You've just sent data from computer A to computer B, and they're on different networks. If they're on the same network, there are no routers, just a switch or two, and the switches operate at Layer 2 and never look at IPs. Just MAC addresses (There are exceptions but let's not go there). The only devices in that scenario that will look at IPs will be the end computers to make sure the packets are meant for them.

I"ve left a ton of information, details, exceptions, etc... out but that's the rough basics that I can type out while I should be working.

It is difficult to cope with low mood. Some people turn to food to manage feelings of sadness or anxiety, so I understand that experience.

When the desire to eat unhealthy food arises, pause, take a deep breath, and close your eyes. Perform a physical scan from head to toe to notice bodily sensations, then reflect on your emotional state and internal thoughts. There is often an underlying emotion and a quiet internal narrative driving the urge to binge. You do not necessarily need to fight it, but you should acknowledge its presence.

If possible, practice delaying gratification. If you crave junk food, tell yourself you will wait 15 minutes. During that time, engage in a distracting or absorbing activity, such as drinking a large glass of water or coffee, or doing something that requires focus. Even engaging in a heated discussion on a political forum can work. The goal is to shift your attention away from the immediate craving. Often, the urge will subside within that timeframe. If it persists, you may eat the food, having honored the agreement you made with yourself. However, each time you successfully delay, increase the waiting period by five minutes. If you resist the urge, decrease the time by five minutes. Over time, you may find a balance where you can endure the wait and move past the craving.
